title: Post-Course Portfolio: Authentication & User Management System
descriptionMarkdown:
# Authentication & User Management System

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone. This project is a prerequisite building block for several later catalog entries (Online Quiz Platform, Forum/Reddit-Style Backend, E-commerce Backend, Project Management App, Food Delivery Backend) that all need real authentication rather than an assumed caller identity — build or at least design this one first.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`credential-store-checkpoint`** ("Hashed credential store"), a pure in-memory `CredentialStore.run(String input)` program. Grading checks only the *observable* register/login/change-password behavior — it cannot verify from the outside which hashing algorithm you actually used, since that is an implementation detail no black-box test can see. **You are still required to implement real, salted PBKDF2 hashing (or bcrypt/Argon2 via a library) internally**, and a source review separately confirms this — passing the behavioral tests alone with, say, plaintext comparison would defeat the entire point of the exercise, even though it might pass the automated cases.

## Beyond what the lessons taught

Spring Security and JWT are not covered by the 25-chapter curriculum, which teaches the underlying concepts (authentication versus authorization, password hashing, secrets handling, object-level authorization) without a specific security framework. Treat learning Spring Security's filter chain and a JWT library as required, deliberate self-directed research for this project, using the official Spring Security reference documentation as your primary source.

## Architecture overview

```text
AuthController                  <- /api/auth/register, /api/auth/login
UserService                      <- your checkpoint's register/login/change rules, reshaped as a Spring bean
User (JPA entity)                <- id, username (UNIQUE), passwordHash, salt
JwtTokenProvider                  <- issues and validates signed tokens (self-directed research)
SecurityFilterChain configuration <- protects resources by role and by ownership
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a service.** Carry your register/login/change-password rules (with real PBKDF2 hashing) into `UserService`, unit tests unchanged.
2. **Slice 2 — persistence with a real unique constraint.** `User` entity with `username` as `UNIQUE`; a duplicate registration attempt must fail at the database level, not just in application code.
3. **Slice 3 — Spring Security and JWT.** Wire up a `SecurityFilterChain`, issue a JWT on successful login, and protect at least one endpoint requiring authentication.
4. **Slice 4 — role-based authorization.** Add an `ADMIN`-only endpoint and confirm a non-admin authenticated user is rejected with `403`, not `401`.
5. **Slice 5 — object-level authorization.** Add a "my profile" endpoint that only the authenticated user's own record may access, verified against the token's identity, never a client-supplied id.

## Common pitfalls

- **Comparing passwords as plain strings "just to get the tests passing."** This defeats the entire purpose of the project; always hash-and-verify, even though a naive test suite might not catch the difference.
- **Confusing 401 (not authenticated at all) with 403 (authenticated but not authorized).** Return the correct one for each case; conflating them makes debugging a real client integration much harder.
- **Trusting a client-supplied user id for "my profile" instead of the id embedded in the validated token.** This is exactly the object-level-authorization gap Chapter 23 warns about.
- **Logging the raw password or the full JWT on a failed login attempt "for debugging."** Apply the redaction discipline from Chapter 23's own lab to every log line touching credentials.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Register a user, log in, and inspect the returned JWT's payload (base64-decode it yourself) to confirm it contains only what you intended (never a password or hash).
- Attempt to access another user's "my profile" data using your own valid token but a different user's id in the URL, and confirm a clear authorization rejection.
- Let a token expire (set a very short expiry for this test) and confirm a request with it is rejected, not silently accepted.
- Grep your own application logs after a full test run for the literal password strings you used, and confirm zero matches.

## Required evidence

- A password-hashing test confirming two hashes of the same password differ (due to salting) and both still verify.
- An authorization test matrix: unauthenticated request rejected, authenticated-but-wrong-role request rejected, authenticated-and-correct-role request accepted, and a request for another user's own-resource data rejected even though the caller is authenticated.
- A test confirming an expired token is rejected, not silently accepted.
- Evidence that no password, hash, or token ever appears in application logs, using the redaction discipline from Chapter 23.
- A threat-model note (assets, actors, entry points) for this specific service, per Chapter 23's Lesson 1.

## Review and completion

A reviewer registers two accounts, logs in as one, and attempts to read or modify the other account's protected resource using a syntactically valid but unauthorized token — this must fail with the correct status, not a stack trace, and the object-level check (not merely the presence of a valid token) must be what stops it.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded credential store checkpoint with real salted PBKDF2 hashing, verified by source review, not just observable behavior
Issue, validate, and expire JWTs correctly, including a tested rejection of an expired token
Distinguish authentication failure (401), role-based authorization failure (403), and object-level authorization failure as three separate, separately-tested outcomes
Keep secrets, hashes, and tokens out of logs using the same redaction discipline as the security chapter
Research and apply a real security framework (Spring Security) beyond what the lessons taught, using its official documentation
